standard.title: Features that influence text preferences
standard.description: analyse how features of literary texts influence readers' preference for texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain how literary devices and language features create character and influence emotions and opinions (AC9E7LE03). They have not yet analysed how the combination of text features shapes readers' preferences and judgements about literary value.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse how features of literary texts — characterisation, setting, plot, theme and literary devices — influence readers' preference for texts.

nodes.label: Features that create preference
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify specific literary features that create a personal preference response and explain why those features appeal or do not appeal.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two literary features (e.g. characterisation, pacing, setting) that contribute to your preference for or against a text, and explain how each feature shapes your response.
nodes.typical_width: Reflect on and discuss responses to literature including characterisation, setting, plot events, themes and literary devices — connecting each to factors that influence preference.
wider: Survey peer preferences for the same text and compare which features create different responses — examining whether preference factors are personal, cultural or conventional
Compare the features that create preference in a literary text versus a popular/genre text, examining what different reader communities value

response_modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of analysable literary features to move beyond 'I liked/didn't like it'. Range of feature types — across characterisation, setting, plot, theme, device — matters before students can analyse preference with precision.

success_criteria: Student names specific literary features (not just 'the story') as preference-drivers
Student explains how a feature creates the preference — connecting the feature to a reading experience
nodes.hinge_reason: Students with no analytical vocabulary for literary features cannot contribute substantively to collaborative criteria-building at N2 — discussion collapses to preference assertions without feature-grounded analysis.

nodes.label: Collaborative analysis of literary value
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can contribute to and benefit from collaborative discussion of literary preference, formulating shared or contested criteria for literary value.
nodes.minimum_width: In discussion with others, compare factors that influence your preference for a text and identify at least one criterion about what distinguishes literary value that emerges from the discussion.
nodes.typical_width: Collaboratively formulate a list of factors that distinguish literary value — through discussion of characterisation, setting, plot events, themes and literary devices — recognising that criteria may vary between readers.
wider: Compare literary value criteria developed by the class with critical criteria used in published literary awards or reviews, examining overlaps and gaps
Examine how different cultural communities may hold different criteria for literary value, and what this reveals about the relationship between culture and aesthetic judgement

response_modes.reason: Formulating shared criteria from collaborative discussion requires students to integrate their own preference analysis with others' perspectives into provisional shared judgements. The social dimension of literary evaluation — how value is negotiated — is the integrative insight.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Moving from personal preference to criteria for literary value is intellectually rich for Y9 — it connects aesthetic judgement to cultural and social context. Advancing students can engage with the concept that literary value is not fixed but historically and culturally negotiated.
success_criteria: Student contributes at least one preference factor to collaborative discussion with textual grounding
Student can articulate at least one shared or contested criterion that emerged from discussion
